articles.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
articles.summary: The latest figures mark a major milestone as Beijing grapples with an ageing population.
articles.full_text:
Image source, VCG via Getty Images By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 27 October 2026 
Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said. 
Official data released in the last week , external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%. 
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole. 
The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say. 
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children . 
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population. 
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under. 
No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy. 
The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said. 
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying. 
The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. 
It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Birth rates in China have been falling for years now 
China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy , which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015. 
The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested. 
The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said. 
But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows. 
Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said. 
Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year. 
Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures. 
The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier. 
The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited. 
Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants. 
It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

articles.title: Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China
articles.summary: The France star had referred to the former Chinese leader as a "dictator" during an interview about memes.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
A backlash has erupted on Chinese social media over Mbappé's comments on a "Chinese dictator" By Kelly Ng 
- Published 27 October 2026 
Kylian Mbappé has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands. 
Mbappé had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao. 
The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football. 
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement. 
"I apologise to everyone my words have upset." 
Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans". 
The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead. 
A few people came out in support of him on Chinese social media, but that is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics. 
Few topics are as sensitive as Mao, which may explain why brands were so quick to terminate partnerships with a global sports star like Mbappé. 
The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview hosted by Real Madrid's Aurélien Tchouaméni first aired. In clips that have been circulating online, Mbappé does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time". 
The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people". 
Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid. 
But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator". 
Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people". 
Many people are therefore also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more. 
Image source, Weibo Image caption, 
Weibo users are recirculating the clip by blurring the meme and redacting references to Mao 
What is the reaction in China? 
Chinese fans have been criticising Mbappé – who is popular in China and has huge brand endorsements – of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public". 
"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," reads another comment on Weibo. 
As the anger online grew louder, Chinese brands began to cut ties, although they did not explicitly refer to the video. 
The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people". 
Drinks giant Dongpeng issued a similar statement: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments." 
According to state-owned newspaper The Global Times, state broadcaster CCTV's news apps will not feature content related to the French striker. CCTV will also stop showing La Liga matches, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. Real Madrid is one of 20 clubs that play in the Spanish football league and is the most decorated team with 36 league titles. 
China's foreign ministry has also weighed in, with spokesperson Lin Jian saying: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society." 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Mbappé has a significant commercial presence in China 
China is a major market for international sports stars and homegrown brands have signed multimillion-dollar endorsement contracts with Mbappé, Norwegian striker Erling Haaland, and NBA player Stephen Curry. 
By 14:00 local time on Tuesday, five of the top 10 trending topics on Weibo centered on Mbappé, with the hashtag "multiple brands terminate partnerships with Mbappé" topping the list. 
"Don't ever come to China," read one of the top comments on Weibo. 
Why is Mao a sensitive topic? 
Mao founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s. 
His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party. 
His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach. 
So jokes or memes about Mao are seen not just as an insult to the party but also its closely-guarded narrative about the country's past. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Mbappé has said some of the memes "reveal a lack of political and human awareness" 
It's unclear when the Mbappé meme involving Mao began but his nickname, "the dictator", has made the striker the subject of many memes and jokes online. 
Mbappé is widely regarded as one of the best footballers in the world and has wielded significant influence at the clubs he has played for. His extraordinary speed, goalscoring ability and worldwide popularity have made him a global icon, attracting millions of fans, major sponsorship deals and media attention, with his influence extending into fashion, culture and business. 
In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches, leading to more jokes about the nickname. 
France teammate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup, calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades. 
In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people". 
"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history," he said. 
"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life." 
Additional reporting by Fan Wang and Osmond Chia

articles.title: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party
articles.summary: The highly secretive four-day Plenum starts Monday in Beijing.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Plenums are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year By Stephen McDonell 
China correspondent 
- Published 26 October 2026 
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come. 
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks. 
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges. 
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after. 
What is a plenum? 
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year. 
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities. 
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed. 
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite. 
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits. 
What is on the agenda this year? 
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao. 
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal. 
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel. 
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials. 
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party. 
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled. 
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality". 
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down. 
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general. 
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

articles.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
articles.summary: The Villa Vie Odyssey suspended its voyage and is working with passengers on "temporary living arrangements".
articles.full_text:
Image source, Villa Vie Residences Image caption, 
The Villa Vie Odyssey was more than 750 days into its voyage around the world when it came to a stop in Cambodia By Koh Ewe   and   Claire Graham ,  BBC News NI 
- Published 28 October 2026 
A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia. 
The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements". 
It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world". 
Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (£6,000) from $1,800. 
Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs". 
"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said. 
The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said. 
There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres. 
The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website. 
Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds. 
The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia. 
Passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told the BBC they were informed by Villa Vie Residences' chief executive at 6am on Tuesday that they had to leave by 2pm on the same day. 
The couple said passengers had known for some time about the company's financial difficulties. A potential investor had previously come onboard the ship to do due dilligence, but in the end it did not work out. 
"Even then, we were still hoping a miracle investor would come through," they said. "Although there were signs that this would happen, we still felt disbelief when it became real. We were heartbroken. It felt like our dream had been crushed." 
"There have been a lot of hugs and tears as residents support one another and process what has happened." 
Another passenger Holly Hennessey said that the ship's passengers had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed". 
Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said. 
"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," Hennessey told the BBC from Cambodia. 
"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting." 
Canen and Bodin said the location in Cambodia was "a difficult place to disembark" because of the distance to a major international airport. 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
Cruise passenger Holly Hennessey and her cat, Captain, have now found themselves in Cambodia 
During their time onboard the Villa Vie Odyssey, passengers had access to several bars and restaurants, a pool deck and a pickleball court, according to its website. 
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month. 
Last year, the company launched a lifetime residence programme for people to spend their retirement years at sea. 
In 2024, days after US President Donald Trump won his second term, Villa Vie Residences announced a four-year "Skip Forward" package. 
Its CEO told Fox Business at the time that it was the "perfect product for those who said they'd leave the country if 'XYZ' wins the election". 
For Canen and Bodin the experience was "worth it", despite the fact it was shorter than expected. 
"We loved our two years on Odyssey—the adventures, the places we visited and the friends we made along the way." 
Many of the passengers have already made plans to "settle together off the ship, so those friendships and that sense of community are continuing on land", they said. 
The couple plans to spend a few days in Sihanoukville, before travelling to different parts of South East Asia while they "figure out our next chapter". 
But others, like Hennessey, have decided to stick around in Cambodia in the hopes that the Odyssey will set sail again soon. 
"Until they say we are done - done done - I am not giving up. I could never duplicate this lifestyle. The idea of going home? It would be so trite," she said. 
"Cambodia's not the worst place to hang out." 
Additional reporting by Thanya Doksone.

articles.title: India and China were easing tensions - then a border official spoke out
articles.summary: India-China ties were on a cautious recovery path until a border official’s remarks raised fresh doubts about ground realities.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
India and China have a fragile thaw in relations since the 2020 clashes By Anbarasan Ethirajan Global affairs correspondent 
- Published 28 October 2026 
For much of the past year, India-China relations appeared to be on a cautious path to recovery. 
The two countries have seen ups and downs in their ties over decades - especially over the disputed Himalayan frontier. 
But events of the past few days suggest that the thaw which has followed their most recent clashes in 2020 may be more fragile than it seems. 
The latest concerns began when India's border police chief said Chinese troops had returned to disputed areas along the Himalayan frontier in large numbers earlier this year, pitching tents several kilometres inside territory claimed by India. 
The remarks by Shatrujeet Singh Kapur, director general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), have triggered a political controversy in Delhi. 
To begin with, such comments by serving officials are rare. Sensitive border issues are usually addressed by the federal government through its defence or foreign ministries. 
At a recent gathering of officers in Rajasthan state, Kapur said face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops had taken place at several locations in the north-eastern state of Arunachal Pradesh and were continuing. 
The confrontations began in July, he said, but both sides initially withdrew. 
A few days later, Chinese troops returned in larger numbers and pitched tents "around six-to-seven kilometres inside India's perception of the Line of Actual Control (LAC)", he added. 
The LAC is an ill-defined line separating the areas controlled by the neighbours and India and China have sparred for decades over this disputed 3,440km (2,100-mile) border. 
China claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of southern Tibet. But Delhi has always rejected the claim, saying the state was an integral part of India. 
The dispute is one of the most persistent challenges inherited by independent India from the British colonial rule in 1947. It led to a brief border war in 1962, in which India suffered a humiliating defeat. 
More than six decades later, much of the frontier remains undemarcated, with the two countries maintaining overlapping territorial claims. 
The region's rugged terrain adds to the challenge: shifting river courses, lakes and snow-covered peaks make it difficult to establish a clear boundary. 
As a result, troops from the two sides can find themselves face-to-face along the frontier, sometimes triggering violent clashes and diplomatic tensions. 
Image source, Anbarasan Ethirajan/BBC Image caption, 
India and China share an ill-defined border demarcated by mountains, rivers and lakes 
The last major escalation came in June 2020 , when Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in Ladakh. At least 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese soldiers were killed. 
It was the first fatal confrontation between the two sides since 1975. Indian opposition parties accused the government of losing territory to China - a claim Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has repeatedly rejected. 
The clashes triggered a sharp deterioration in relations, disrupting diplomatic engagement and affecting trade and travel. After several rounds of negotiations, the neighbours agreed in 2024 to take steps towards easing border tensions. 
They have since moved to restore direct flights and ease visa restrictions imposed after the clashes. 
Chinese President Xi Jinping also visited India in September for the Brics summit, his first visit to the country in seven years. 
These developments raised hopes of a broader normalisation of ties. But the latest reported stand-offs have renewed questions about how much progress has actually been made on the ground. 
After Kapur's comments, the main opposition Congress party once again accused Modi of making concessions to Beijing. 
"The prime minister and his entire apparatus remain silent on this grave issue," senior Congress leader Jairam Ramesh wrote on X , external . 
The Indian government has not explicitly denied Kapur's account that Chinese troops had pitched tents several kilometres inside what India considers to be its side of the LAC. 
Foreign ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said last week that "the situation in the border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns". 
He said both countries were using military and diplomatic channels to address outstanding issues, but gave no further details. 
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesman said that China had "consistently and strictly adhered to relevant agreements" reached with India and it conducted "normal patrol and management activities in the border areas to safeguard territorial sovereignty". 
Image source, LightRocket via Getty Images Image caption, 
The Galwan clashes were the first fatal confrontation between the two sides since 1975 
Experts say Kapur's remarks offer a rare glimpse into what they describe as China's increasingly assertive military posture along the disputed frontier. 
"This pattern of Chinese probing at various points of the Arunachal Pradesh border has been happening for some time," Shyam Saran, a former Indian foreign secretary who led several rounds of border talks with China in the mid-2000s, told the BBC. 
He said such actions were "not enough to result in an immediate war, but enough to sort of create new facts on the ground". 
Indian opposition parties have long accused China of extending its presence in both Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh, leading to tensions. 
Zhou Bo, a retired senior colonel in China's People's Liberation Army who is now associated with Tsinghua University in Beijing, said both countries had learnt lessons from the 2020 Galwan clashes. 
"The two sides should be more careful to avoid this kind of thing from happening in the future," he said, adding that Chinese media had not reported on the latest stand-offs in Arunachal Pradesh. 
India and China's tensions also come against the backdrop of a complicated economic relationship. 
Despite their differences, the countries remain major trading partners, with bilateral trade , external reaching $151bn last year. But the balance is heavily tilted in Beijing's favour, with Chinese exports to India accounting for about $131bn. 
India continues to rely on Chinese imports for machinery, rare earth magnets, electric vehicle batteries and pharmaceutical products. 
This dependence means tensions with Beijing can have consequences well beyond the border, particularly for Indian industries and infrastructure projects. 
Last week, China also announced restrictions on exports of tunnel-boring machines used in metro rail and highway construction, saying they were intended to protect national security and national interests. Although these curbs were not India specific, they would have a bearing on India's infrastructure push. 
"Chinese policy towards India is designed to complicate India's rise, including India's ability to master certain things in advanced technology and manufacturing," Christopher Clary, a professor at the University at Albany in New York, told the BBC. 
A similar problem emerged last year when China restricted export of rare earth magnets - widely used in electric vehicles, smartphones, wind turbines and medical scanners. 
The move temporarily caused supply problems for Indian industries, highlighting how Beijing's control over key materials can affect global supply chains. 
India is now trying to build domestic capacity to produce rare earth magnets, but developing the industry will take time and investment. 
Image source, Anbarasan Ethirajan/BBC Image caption, 
Arunachal Pradesh has long been the focus of tension between India and China 
For people living along the disputed frontier, the consequences of tensions with China are more immediate. 
"Villagers living in some border areas tell us that they cannot access grazing lands because of Chinese intrusion and encroachment. It's not something new, it's been happening for a long time," says Tongam Rina, a senior journalist with the Arunachal Times. 
This has created a "sense of insecurity among the people here," she adds. 
Villagers usually do not return to those "prohibited" areas for hunting and yak rearing, and they are not sure when they would be allowed again. 
The border dispute also has wider strategic implications for Delhi, with a growing realisation that President Donald Trump's focus on expanding economic engagement with China could limit Washington's willingness to back India in any future confrontation with Beijing. 
China may have little interest in a full-scale conflict with India but, analysts say, it could see advantages in allowing the dispute to continue. 
As China's economic and military power grows, it may calculate that a prolonged stalemate will strengthen its position in any future negotiations. 
For India, the latest stand-offs are a reminder that improved diplomatic ties do not necessarily translate into lasting stability along the border.

articles.title: India's largest share sale could end cheap mobile internet for millions
articles.summary: Jio's IPO promises a windfall for investors, but could signal the end of cheap mobile data for millions.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution By Nikhil Inamdar Mumbai 
- Published 27 October 2026 
India's biggest telecom giant, the Meta and Google-backed Jio Platforms, is set to make its stock market debut on Wednesday. 
Despite a bruising spell for Indian markets, its historic $3.2bn initial public offering (IPO) - the country's largest ever - has drawn overwhelming demand from top global fund managers, domestic institutions and mom-and-pop retail investors. 
Bids outstripped the shares on offer within hours of subscriptions opening on 21 October. 
Owned by Asia's richest man, Mukesh Ambani, Jio is one of India's most consequential companies, with half a billion people subscribing to its cheap mobile data. But its meteoric rise has also been dogged by controversy. 
The company burst onto India's crowded telecom scene in 2016, offering throwaway tariffs that got millions of Indians hooked to the internet. 
But its launch led to a huge disruption in the telecom sector. A market once crowded with 17 operators shrunk to an oligopoly of just three, with critics accusing the deep-pocketed company of waging a price war that pushed rivals out of business. 
More recently, Elon Musk criticised Ambani, calling him the "real boss of India", suggesting that Jio was trying to thwart Starlink's entry into India. Reliance dismissed the allegations saying it welcomed competition ‌from Musk. 
For all the scrutiny it has faced over the last decade, Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution , spawning a huge digital economy and democratising online payments, food delivery and e-commerce in Asia's third-biggest economy. 
Within three years of its launch, customer data usage rose fifty-fold and data prices crashed. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Jio's cheap tariffs democratised internet use in India a decade ago 
This aggressive discounting helped Jio rapidly amass some 553 million mobile subscribers by 2026. It also cemented its dominance in other segments, capturing 50% of the wireless broadband market and more than 40% of fixed broadband. 
Jio also carries 60% of India's wireless data traffic and boasts of the largest 5G subscriber base outside China, according to brokerage Emkay Global, which has described the company as the "digital engine of India". 
But analysts say its stock market debut - which will see its promoters dilute their shareholding by about 3% - could mark a turning point in Jio's pricing strategy, potentially bringing an end to years of ultra-cheap tariffs. 
"The era of Jio using cheap tariffs as a market-share weapon is drawing to a close," said Nitya Shah, co-founder of KamayaKya Wealth Management. 
"A listed Jio must answer to minority shareholders… which structurally reduces its incentive to keep pricing suppressed." 
Jio's future growth will no longer be driven primarily by adding subscribers through discounted plans. Instead, it will depend on "earning more per subscriber - through the migration to 5G, successive tariff revisions, and the extension of fixed wireless broadband into homes fibre has never reached", brokerage company Motilal Oswal said in a note. 
The listing could also pave the way for Jio's competitors to raise prices, as fears of being undercut by a cheaper rival begin to recede. 
"The biggest beneficiary of this shift could be Vodafone Idea," says Shah. "It is a moment the sector's weakest balance sheet gets its strongest tailwind". 
For Indian consumers, any further increases would come on the heels of an industry-wide tariff hike a few years ago. Analysts say another round of price rises could trigger a fresh churn in the market as price-sensitive customers switch to the cheapest plans available. 
While consumers may have to brace for higher bills, Jio's IPO offers investors a bet on India's seemingly insatiable appetite for data - and the growing ecosystem of digital services the company offers across entertainment, cloud computing, gaming and financial services. 
India has emerged as the second-largest consumer of mobile data in the world, driven by lower tariffs and rising penetration of smartphones. 
Jio's monthly data use per customer has climbed from 28.7 GB in 2024 to 42.3 GB in 2026 - up by 52% in two years. As per some estimates, usage is expected to surge further to 65GB by the end of this decade as disposable incomes rise. 
All of this will give a tailwind for Jio to drive long-term growth in average revenue per user. 
"Penetration of most digital services remains well below China and the US, which leaves significant headroom [for growth]," according to Emkay Global. 
The listing is also likely to enhance transparency and provide investors with a "clearer market valuation" for the company, according to Moody's rating agency, as Jio is currently part of Reliance Industries, which has businesses spanning oil refining and retail. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
At $3.2bn, the Jio Platforms IPO is India's biggest share sale 
But as much as its central and growing role in India's economy has excited investors, the buzz about the IPO also comes from the fact that this is the first share sale from the Reliance conglomerate in over two decades. 
The company - which started as a small spice and polyester yarn trading venture in 1958 before expanding into textiles, petrochemicals, refining and eventually to retail, telecom and digital services - is known for its track record of long-term wealth creation, and enjoys legendary status among mom-and-pop investors. 
Dhirubhai Ambani , the founder of the Reliance empire, is said to have played a foundational role in popularising equity investing and taking it beyond the preserve of traders and wealthy families in the 1980s and 90s. 
In its early years, Reliance built a vast base of individual shareholders by turning its annual general meetings into grand spectacles of big announcements, dividend payouts and celebrations of public share ownership. Over time, this helped forge a fiercely loyal investor base, many of whom developed a deep emotional bond with the company. 
And while Reliance Industries' stock has fallen nearly 20% over the past year, its longer-term track record continues to inspire confidence. 
"The company has given average annualised returns of around 30% consistently for thirty years," Kranthi Bathini of Mumbai-based WealthMills Securities told the BBC. 
"That's why there's anticipation that the same magic can be replicated with the Jio IPO."

articles.title: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
articles.summary: The King is on a nine-day tour that will take him to three countries, including the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
King addresses 'suffering and injustices' in Bahamas past By Daniela Relph ,  Royal correspondent ,  Reporting from Nassau   and   Henry Moore 
- Published 27 October 2026 Updated 28 October 2026 
King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations. 
Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices. 
His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery. 
The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit. 
Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations. 
Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour. 
King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973. 
The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC. 
A small group of protesters gathered close to the rally shouting "pay us what you owe us" and "return artefacts you've stolen." 
The group of around a dozen protesters was kept outside the main venue as they called on the King to help change the UK government's position on apologising and offering reparations. 
"He's a man of influence. The Crown still has influence. And if they do not do it then we will become a republic and we will turn our backs on England if you do not show respect to the former colonies," said one protester, Sharon Purcer-Cooper. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The King spoke with young people as he attended his first engagement of the trip 
Image source, PA Image caption, 
The King spoke to these performers at a Nassau rally where the focus was on youth 
Image source, PA Image caption, 
The King spoke with Philip Edward Davis, Prime Minister of the Bahamas 
During his speech in Nassau, the King acknowledged his 50-year-long commitment to fighting climate change and highlighted the challenges faced by low-lying Caribbean islands, saying that "our world cries out for healing". 
He went on to call on young people at the rally to "take up the sacred task to play your part" as "in years to come, this will be surely be the measure of every person - how they answered the call to care for planet earth - the source of our life, our prosperity and our security". 
The King resumes engagements in the Bahamas on Wednesday, where he will hear how vulnerable the low lying islands of the Caribbean are to climate change. 
He will also learn more about the Bahamian tradition of Junkanoo - a cultural festival and street parade. 
Buckingham Palace said opportunities for the King to reflect on the legacy of the slave trade will be built into the schedule of his nine-day tour of three Caribbean countries with visits planned to memorials and other places of reflection and remembrance. 
A spokesperson for the palace told the BBC that the King's programme on the tour "will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future", specifically those which are "having a transformative effect on the region". 
For the King, the spokesperson added, the "tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past". 
Those themes will be reflected by the King through the nine-day visit, the palace said. 
The visit has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations. 
The King will move to Guyana later this week where his engagements will focus on the environment and biodiversity. 
He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth. 
The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

articles.title: Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America
articles.summary: The Trump-Lula relationship may have thawed, but several issues could reignite tensions between the two leaders.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Ione Wells 
- Published 27 October 2026 
"Brazil will not accept being anyone's backyard," Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva declared in his election victory speech, a message squarely aimed at Washington. 
Domestic elections are rarely won on foreign policy, and this one was no different. But Lula's defiance against what he has described as US interference in Brazilian affairs evoked a patriotic spirit that proved an effective campaigning tool. 
It also chimed with his wider brand of politics as a former union leader: standing up to powerful figures. 
Paradoxically, it seems to have earned him President Donald Trump's respect. "I like Lula, we get along well," Trump said, responding to the result. "I didn't take sides," he added, before calling the election "terrible" and "rigged". 
Figure caption, 
Watch: How President Lula turned it around to beat Flávio Bolsonaro 
If that sounds muddled, it is because the relationship between the two men is not straightforward. Trump did not explicitly endorse Lula's rival Flávio Bolsonaro, who refused to recognise the result. But Trump was a close ally of Flávio's father, the former President Jair Bolsonaro. 
When I spoke to Lula at his residence about a year ago, relations had hit rock bottom. He told me he had "no relationship" with Trump, that they had never spoken, and that he had no intention of picking up the phone. Trump had recently imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, largely as a political response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which the US president called a "witch-hunt" . 
Rather than tiptoeing around Trump, as some US allies did, Lula fought back – and it paid off. 
He made fiery speeches invoking Brazilian sovereignty, attacked US interference in the judicial process, and took to wearing a blue cap reading "Brazil belongs to Brazilians". 
His approval ratings jumped. 
He accused the Bolsonaro family, who had lobbied for the tariffs, of being unpatriotic – a blow to a political right that so often claims patriotism as its terrain. 
Even some in the agricultural lobby, typically strong Bolsonaro supporters but reliant on US trade, thought Lula had a point. 
The US eventually backed down and reduced the tariffs, although they have since risen again. 
Relations then improved. 
The two men spoke at the United Nations and later met in the Oval Office, where Trump called the talks "very good" and Lula said he left "very satisfied". 
Another indication, perhaps, that Trump likes a strong leader. 
- 
Fireworks heard after Lula's victory in São Paulo 
- Published 2 days ago 
So why might Trump be unhappy with the result? 
Latin America has swung to the right, with Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, Argentina and Peru all electing presidents closely aligned with the Trump administration. Trump has sought to use these allies to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere, a strategy he has dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine". 
Christopher Sabatini, senior fellow for Latin America at Chatham House, notes that Trump thought Brazil would be the "10th and biggest prize" after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round. 
Brazil is Latin America's largest economy, and the younger Bolsonaro was expected to join Trump's "Shield of Americas" coalition against narco-trafficking. 
Brazil also holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals after China, and the US had been eyeing preferential access. 
The relationship has thawed, but with four more years ahead for Lula, several issues could reignite tensions. 
Brazil accused the US earlier this year of trying to cast doubt on its electoral system and denied visas to two state department officials planning to visit. 
The US called this "baseless" and revoked the Brazilian ambassador's visa in response. 
If Trump keeps calling this result "rigged", further diplomatic fallout is likely. 
Lula has also vehemently opposed US military action in the region, from the seizure of Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela to the bombing of alleged drug-trafficking vessels. 
He lambasted Washington for designating Brazil's two major gangs as terrorist organisations after lobbying from Flávio Bolsonaro, and warned of attacks on Brazilian sovereignty. 
It is a sensitive subject for a political left that remembers the region's brutal 20th Century dictatorships, many backed by the CIA in the name of stopping communism. 
Then there is US tech. 
Lula's campaign accused Meta of favouring Flávio Bolsonaro. 
Meta denied this but admitted moderation issues and technical errors had wrongly removed some posts or limited their reach. 
Lula's supporters responded by sharing his messages through a 10-million-strong WhatsApp group to bypass the algorithms. 
Separately, the Trump administration is unhappy with Pix, Brazil's instant payment system, which has boosted the economy, but which the US sees as taking business from Visa and Mastercard. 
The relationship has exposed political divisions. 
In the campaign, Bolsonaro supporters waved US flags at their rallies and, in one case, an inflatable saying "Trump Nuke Brazil", while Lula and his supporters accused Flávio Bolsonaro of protecting US interests over Brazil's. 
Still, tensions can be overstated. 
The US remains Brazil's second-biggest trading partner after China, and for now the two leaders get on. 
Whether that lasts will depend on how far the US tries to intervene in Brazilian affairs, and how bullish Lula is in response.

articles.title: Ex-wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president freed after collapse of attempted murder case
articles.summary: Marry Mubaiwa had been held on remand for seven years after being charged in 2019 for her then husband's attempted murder.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Marry Mubaiwa in an image from 2018 when she was still married to Constantino Chiwenga By Patrick Jackson 
- Published 27 October 2026 
The former wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president has been freed from remand after seven years while on trial for his attempted murder. 
Marry Mubaiwa was charged in 2019, after her then husband Gen Constantino Chiwenga accused her of trying to impede his medical treatment in South Africa. 
Ordering her release, a magistrate said Mubaiwa had suffered mental, physical and financial prejudice during the trial, state-owned daily the Herald said. 
The ruling was made after the state asked for the trial to be postponed by a month in order to engage witnesses. 
Her lawyer described the ruling as a victory that had come too late, because her client's rights had been violated by the delay in the trial. 
Speaking outside court in the capital Harare on Tuesday, the lawyer added that if the state moved for a new trial, they would deal with it when it happened. 
Mubaiwa was accused of attempting to kill Chiwenga, while he was in hospital in Pretoria. The vice-president then went to China for four months of treatment. 
Mubaiwa was remanded in custody and denied bail. 
According to the New Zimbabwe news website, Mubaiwa celebrated her release outside court, and said justice had been achieved and that she was proud of her lawyer. 
In 2017, Chiwenga played a key role in overthrowing then President Robert Mugabe.
